Better Harness, Better Answers

Document Intelligence Without Bigger Models

Nirant Kasliwal

Open with the claim you will test: with one small model, how far can the code around the model move the answers? We did not swap in a larger model, so this talk measures only what the harness adds. Every number comes from logged runs.

Keep this under thirty seconds. I help companies evaluate, optimize and deploy agents, so I spend my days reading agent traces, and most of what I show today comes from that habit. My last talk, The Agent as Compiler, argued that the harness around a model deserves engineering attention. Today I put numbers on one harness, on real documents, with one small model.

One small model stays locked. Only the harness changes.

3

The experiment is simple to state. Freeze the model and every sampling setting. These runs use the 4-bit weights hosted by Darkbloom, because a 20-question run took 17 minutes at best on our laptop and 3 to 13 hosted, and we wanted three runs of everything. The same model in Ollama, nvfp4 at 7.6 GB, runs on a 32 GB laptop. Change one part of the harness, then re-score every question. Because the model never changes, any difference comes from the code around it, or from the run-to-run noise we will measure.

4

Annual reports, contracts, regulations, technical orders with line drawings, and French statistics. Twenty questions are for validation, and we read their failures while building. Twenty more are the test set: no change came from them. Both sets search the same pages, so they differ only in their questions. Multi-hop questions need reasoning across up to three pages. The corpus is deliberately small; every score here is at this scale.

Why is this hard?

The answer is not text

1  The page is a scan

A scanned table holds no text for search to match.

2  The value is in a chart

A bar has a height, not a number.

3  The label is in a drawing

A part’s name exists only as ink on a diagram.

The answer is not where search looks

4  The wording differs

The question says B gas. The report says gaz B.

5  The proof is an absence

No retrieved passage can show a clause is missing.

6  The answer spans pages

One page points to the next. None holds it all.

Ask first: why would a question about a PDF be hard at all? Most people say the model. All six of these happen before the model reasons about anything. Either it never received the fact, or it received the wrong passages. The top row is a document processing problem. The bottom row is a search problem. The next two slides show a real page for each one.

6

Read each question aloud and ask how a text search would find the answer. It cannot. The scanned page has zero characters behind it. The chart’s value is a bar height, and LightOnOCR estimates 50 from it. The drawing’s PDF text holds only the caption, yet LightOnOCR lists the labels, including safety pin stowage bracket. These three end the argument about whether you need OCR. The chart question is in our validation set. The scan comes from XL-DocBench and the drawing from ViDoRe v3, and we ran those two separately as a demonstration: none of our 40 scored questions has its answer only on a scan or a drawing, which is a limit of the test sets. Run separately, on Qwen3.5-9B fp4 through Darkbloom: the grep agent over the PDF text layer answered not_found on both the scan and the drawing, and the same agent over the merged Markdown answered both correctly, with 1.5 m and the safety pin stowage bracket.

The answer is not where search looks

4 THE WORDING DIFFERS

Which country supplies all of France’s B gas?

“gaz B”, “Pays-Bas”: no shared word

Programmation pluriannuelle de l’énergie, p. 101

5 THE PROOF IS AN ABSENCE

Does the Cremer-Ultragenyx supply agreement contain a non-compete clause?

“Compete” appears nowhere in it

Ultragenyx supply agreement, p. 1

6 THE ANSWER SPANS PAGES

A fuel checklist points to one order for ESDS items. How far from the wire is the heat source held?

The checklists name this order. It holds the distance.

TO 00-25-234, p. 68

Here the text exists and search still misses it. The French report shares no words with the English question. The contract question has no matching clause at all, and top-five retrieval returns the nearest thing, exclusivity, as if it were the answer. The third needs two hops: the checklist names TO 00-25-234, and only that order holds the distance. Look closely at the highlighted line. The PDF text stores five with a single f-i ligature character, so a plain search for the word five finds nothing there. The OCR Markdown spells it normally. PDF text can lose an answer even when it looks perfect.

9

Read it left to right. Docling with OCR off, on every page, is our 1x. It is not Docling’s best configuration. Then we split pages by type. pymupdf4llm, a library built on PyMuPDF, reads the characters stored in the PDF and writes them as Markdown for text pages. LightOnOCR-3, a vision model, reads a picture of scan, chart and drawing pages, so it never sees those stored characters. A page goes to the vision model when it holds under 200 characters of text, images over 10 percent of the page, or 40 or more vector drawings. Words improve 3.3 times but numbers only 1.4 times, because OCR misses things: on its pages, 21.9 percent of the numbers PyMuPDF can extract were gone. Last, PyMuPDF extracts each line of the page, we check it against the OCR Markdown, and any line holding a word or number the Markdown lacks is restored to the page. This is plain counting, with no model. That is 15 times fewer words lost and 12 times fewer numbers lost, or about 5 and 9 times against the same pipeline without this step. The block sits on LightOnOCR-3 because that is where this recovers text. pymupdf4llm pages already came from PyMuPDF’s text, so there it adds much less. On the 531 pages, 2,073 of 2,960 lines restored to vision pages had at least half their words absent from the page, against 217 of 1,441 on pymupdf4llm pages. One mismatched word pulls in a whole line, so some restored lines are near-duplicates. A real recovery: on a page of a hydraulic charts document the model left out the printed instruction “Connect with a straightedge the given culvert diameter or height”. In plain terms, words lost go 6.7, 2.1, 0.5 percent and numbers lost 16.4, 12.0, 1.4 percent. The last column keeps 99.6 percent of words and 98.6 percent of numbers, where Docling keeps 93.3 and 83.6, so small losses make these ratios look large. This metric treats PyMuPDF’s text as truth, so it says nothing about charts and scans. For charts we ran ParseBench on its 568 chart pages: LightOnOCR-3 at our 2 megapixel setting passes 58.3 percent of data-point rules, against 1.1 percent for pymupdf4llm alone. Its published 64.7 uses 5 megapixels, so expect a gap at our setting. We chose it from this measurement, not from the test questions.

10

Search starts with embedding over 512-token chunks, and BM25 adds exact keyword matching over the same chunks. Hybrid means embedding plus BM25, merged with reciprocal rank fusion, RRF, without tuned weights, keeping the top 5. This step costs almost nothing: about the same token count and no extra model call. Its median across three runs is two questions higher on test. The top-5 limit is still in place.

11

Before you reveal the numbers, ask for a show of hands: does Markdown beat PDF text once you have good search? Here it mostly does not. The grep agent, which the next section explains, calls grep and read tools in a loop. Across three runs its median is 8 of 20 on PDF text and 7 on Markdown, and the runs overlap, 6 to 9 against 7 to 9. Per question it moves both ways: Markdown gains 4 questions and loses 2. BM25 in the loop, the grep agent with BM25 in place of grep, has a median of 9 on both, with runs of 9, 9 and 9 on PDF text and 8 to 10 on Markdown. So why convert at all? Because some answers exist only as pixels. The EU wage chart question, which sits in the validation set, scores nothing on PDF text and full marks on Markdown, with plain RAG, Hybrid RAG and the grep agent, in every run. The scan and the drawing from the start of the talk are the same story, and our scored questions hold few answers like that. Your documents decide how much this matters.

12

Read the question aloud. It asks about biological material, and plain RAG answers cybersecurity, the same way in all three runs. The model is not being careless. It received five chunks, and none of them holds the right category. One chunk begins at the heading for 5.3.4, so that is the category name it saw. The right heading sits higher on the same page, just outside what top-5 retrieval returned. A chunk boundary decided the answer. The grep agent reads the page, sees all four categories and picks the right one, and that is the case for a loop. This is a validation question, shown because the failure is easy to see; the scores in this talk are from the test set.

I expected the fan-out to be the honest middle. It has grep’s reach and no iteration: the model gets one chance to choose search terms. It scored no better than the linear pipe. Whole-corpus keyword reach alone buys nothing here. The gap to the grep agent row is what iteration buys, because the model reads a result and then decides what to look for next. The last row keeps that loop and changes the search tool: BM25 returns the five best passages. Its median is 9, the highest of these four, though its runs overlap the grep agent’s. 14

If the loop matters, does the search inside it matter? We forked the plain grep agent and changed one tool. Same loop, same read tool, same 20-call budget, thinking off. Search now returns the five best passages, by BM25 alone or by Hybrid, in place of every matching line. Across three runs both have a median of 9 of 20 against 7 for grep. The runs overlap, 8–10 against 7–9, and we added these after the test scores were known, so call it a lead and not proof. Neither beats the other on score. Per question it moves both ways again: BM25 gains 5 and loses 5, Hybrid gains 6 and loses 3. On tokens, give both numbers. Against grep, BM25 is −19% median, +34% total: its median question is cheaper and its long questions cost more. Hybrid is +54% median, +67% total. The median answer makes 5.5 searches and 7 reads with grep, 2 and 9.5 with BM25, and 2 and 12 with Hybrid. So if you try one, try BM25: same median as Hybrid, no embedding model and fewer tokens by both measures. If someone asks about the validation questions: BM25 and the grep agent tie at a median of 16. If someone asks about BM25 with our token fixes: we have not run that combination. That is the score. The next section is about cause and cost: what the traces showed and the tokens the fixes saved.

Our tools hide the clause from the grep agent

Contracts under the law of the State of Israel: our first rewrite named 5 of 6, each with a correct quote.

The missed contract, in the PDF. The converter merged clauses 17.9 to 17.11 into one line of 4,248 characters.

What the model saw of that one line

Read showed 600 characters. Search showed 400. Neither gave a warning.

Clause 17.11 starts at character 2,197

Fix: 200 characters around each match, whole lines on read. The fixed agent named all 6.

Local run: Qwen3.5-9B, nvfp4, Ollama, earlier corpus. Question 6, NICE outsourcing agreement, CUAD. Hosted on merged Markdown the long line is gone, and a 6,000-character read limit stops the grep agent instead. Bar drawn to scale. NICE outsourcing agreement, p. 25

15

The last section moved the score. This one is about cause and cost, and it is the most useful for your own work. The score tells you that something failed; the trace tells you why. Our first rewrite added a catalogue, an outline, refusals and quote checks. I blamed the model for this one until I checked. The grep agent did the right thing: it searched for Israel, opened the NICE contract, and searched that file for “governed”. The tool printed the first 400 characters of the matching line and stopped. That cut was mine, added to save context, and it gave the model no sign that anything was missing. This is the most reusable lesson in the talk. After the fix, the agent got this question right in that local run. In three hosted runs on the 531 pages the Markdown is merged, so that long line is gone, and the plain grep agent still missed it, for a sibling reason: its one read of the contract stopped at the 6,000-character output limit, with a marker this time, and the clause sits at character 8,464. It never read further. Every truncation in your tools needs to say that it truncated. Check yours tonight.

16

Our first rewrite also refused repeats: the harness declines a call the model already made. That fix stopped a wasteful read and created a new stall: the grep agent kept hammering a closed door, and every knock used up budget. Question 7 is my favourite. The model tried three times to call a tool named final_answer, which we never gave it. When a model keeps calling a tool you don't have, consider adding it. These traces came from an earlier question set we had kept out of tuning, so once we used them to change the harness that set stopped being a clean test. We picked a second fresh set for the real check. That check comes after this slide: the score barely moved and the tokens fell.

17

Every fix on the last few slides solved the trace it came from, so here is the score on the test questions. As a median across three runs, the grep agent gets 7 of 20 and Grep Token Reduction gets 8. The lowest and highest runs overlap, so that one answer is within the noise. The fixes move single questions in both directions: against the grep agent, Grep Token Reduction gains 4 questions and loses 6. So each story is true and the score barely moves. Tokens are where it shows. Against the grep agent the median question costs 37% less, and one run of 20 questions costs 21% less in total. Say both numbers, because long questions shrink less than short ones. Median turns fall from 20 to 13. This agent keeps the catalogue, refusals and quote checks from our first rewrite, and adds a map of the collection, naming each source and how it words things. It reads several pages in one call and names any page left out, says when a term search came back empty and how many lines hold each word alone, and drops the review turn. My first drafts failed: hard turn limits of six and ten stopped reads short and lost questions. One bug is worth telling. The model sometimes answered correctly, then replied with an empty object at the review, and my harness kept the empty one. A later empty reply no longer erases a correct answer. One measurement warning: I tried caching model replies to save time. A run partly replayed from that cache scored four questions higher than the same version run fresh. I removed the cache. If someone asks about the validation questions: Grep Token Reduction has a median of 13 against 16 for the grep agent, and tokens still fall, 8% on the median question and 28% in total.

Here is every row side by side, now that you have seen where each one comes from. The same model goes from a median of 5 with plain RAG to 9 with BM25 in the loop, from harness changes alone. Same model, same documents, same converted Markdown in every row. Only the way the model uses search changes. These are the test questions: correct answers out of 20, as the median across three runs, with the lowest and highest run in brackets. At temperature 0 plain RAG scored the same in all three runs; the grep agent’s spread is most likely the hosted endpoint varying on long prompts. Plain RAG and the fan-out each have a median of 5. The grep agent has 7, and so does Hybrid RAG in one pass, so a loop alone is not the whole story. Grep Token Reduction has 8, with 37% fewer median tokens and 21% fewer in total. Adding thinking leaves it at 8, with one run at 11. BM25 or Hybrid inside the loop has 9. Adding thinking to BM25 drops it to 6, with one run at 10, for about twice the tokens. The runs overlap throughout, so read these as leads, not proof. If someone asks about the validation questions: the same lift shows there, plain RAG 9 and the grep agent and BM25 in the loop 16. The two thinking rows are the one dial I have not explained yet, so that comes next.

Thinking does not lift the agents’ medians

Test 20

19

Hover a dot for its run, and click a row to focus it. The same model has one more dial, and here is why I run everything three times. My first run with thinking on scored 13 of 20 on the test set, and I nearly built this slide around it. That run had a 4,096-token output limit, and thinking shares that limit, which also starved the fan-out of any search terms. At 16,384 tokens, Grep Token Reduction scored 11, 8 and 8 against 8, 7 and 8 without thinking. So its median across three runs stays at 8 of 20 and its best run rises to 11, at similar tokens: a median of 94,000 against 98,000 per question, and a total of 2.1 million against 2.2 million per run of 20. BM25 in the loop goes the other way. Its median falls from 9 to 6, with runs of 10, 6 and 5, and its tokens about double: a median of 126,000 to 304,000 per question, and a total of 3.7 million to 5.5 million per run. The median answer with thinking makes 20 calls against 12 without. This agent has no refusals or collection map, which Grep Token Reduction has, and we did not test whether that explains the gap. RAG’s median moves from 5 to 7. The fan-out does not gain: a median of 4 against 5, at three times the tokens. Read that row with care: even at 16,384 tokens, 5 to 7 of its 20 questions per run ended with no search terms, mostly because reasoning used the whole limit. So part of that drop is a limit failure. Thinking also makes results vary between runs, which plain RAG alone does not.

21

Own this before anyone asks. Across three runs hybrid RAG has a median of 7 of the test 20 for under 3,000 tokens per question. The grep agent has the same median for about 155,000 per question and 2.8 million in total per run of 20. BM25 in the loop has 9 for about 126,000 per question and 3.7 million in total. At this model's hosted price that is a fraction of a cent against about a cent per question, which is cheap until you have millions of documents and questions. A sensible system tries the cheap path first. Everything in this talk, all runs and all configurations, cost about sixteen dollars. Run the sums at your own volume.

22

This is the slide people will photograph, so leave it up. OODA is John Boyd's loop: observe, orient, decide, act. Start at the left: three things come before the first loop, because without one-pass scores and frozen fresh questions you can't tell whether anything helped. Convert to Markdown where answers sit in scans, charts or drawings; on our test questions PDF text scored about the same. Teams skip those. Then walk clockwise. Observe: log every call and result, so a stall like read line 204 nine times is visible at all. Orient is the step people rush. Name the layer before you touch anything: documents, search, or how the model uses search. I blamed the model for the Israel clause, and the fault was a silent cut in my own tool. Decide: fix the class, never the one question, and that is why tools now label what they cut or find empty. Act: change one part and retest on fresh questions, in several runs. That step cost me two good stories: one run scored 13 and three more scored 11, 8 and 8, and a run replayed from saved replies scored four questions higher than a fresh one. The fresh traces then show the next failure, and you go round again. The model in the middle never changes.

Change search and the loop before the model

Read the trace to learn why an answer failed.

Documents: CUAD (The Atticus Project, CC BY 4.0), ViDoRe v3 (arXiv 2601.08620), XL-DocBench (arXiv 2608.00036).

23

Two things to take home. First, change how the model searches before you change the model: on the test questions the same model went from a median of 5 with plain RAG to 7 with Hybrid RAG and 9 with BM25 in the loop. Second, tomorrow, open one failed trace from your own system and read it end to end. Traces told us why questions failed and where tokens went, and our fixes cut tokens without raising the score. Then take questions. If someone asks whether a bigger model would help: we did not test one here. The failures we traced were tool, prompt and test-set failures, so fix those first, then measure.

Multi-hop question spans three pages

For outlet-control headwater of a flowing-full concrete box culvert, which equations and chart are used?

Equation 2 sets the head; Charts 8 to 14 solve it p. 10

High tailwater needs Equation 3 as well p. 17

Of those charts, only Chart 8 is concrete box p. 21

Answer: Equation 2 and Equation 3; Chart 8

Plain RAG on PDF text: 2 of 3

Equation 3 and Chart 8

Hybrid RAG: 1 of 3

Chart 8

Trace Fixes: 3 of 3

All three, across 11 calls

Local runs: Qwen3.5-9B, nvfp4, Ollama, earlier corpus. Validation question 16. HEC-5, Hydraulic Charts for the Selection of Highway Culverts, Federal Highway Administration.

FAQ

25

This is what connecting the dots looks like. No single page answers this question. Page 10 says the head comes from Equation 2 and gives a range of charts. Page 17 adds Equation 3 for high tailwater. Page 21 is the only place that says which chart in the range is the concrete box. Top-5 retrieval returns fragments, and the model answers confidently from whichever it received: one of three parts, or two of three. The grep agent can read one page, see that it points elsewhere, and go there. That is the case for a loop over a single shot. On the 531 pages this question stays hard in hosted runs: Grep Token Reduction stops one hop short, naming Charts 8 through 14 and Chart 15 onward in place of Chart 8. Fewer turns can cost you this exact kind of question, so we check it every time.

The harness is a prompt, tools and checks

<role>

<collection>

<file_format>

A printed contents page number is not a line number.

<procedure>

<final_answer>

JSON with a quote for each part of the answer.

FAQ

27

Here are the two maps in full size, because this is where a domain prompt earns its keep. The catalogue comes first: every file with its title, language and page count. Look at the third row. The file name doc_000143 tells the model nothing, and the title tells it everything. Next, the collection section: what each source is and how it words things, such as French reports needing French terms. That is the part you can only write if you know your documents. On the right is the table of contents for one file, built by the outline tool from headings and page markers. The question asks about ESDS items. The outline shows that heading at line 84 on page 2, and line 88 on that page names the next document, TO 00-25-234. That is the first hop of the multi-hop question from earlier. Be honest about this trace: the model did not call outline here. It read the file, asked for pages that do not exist, and the hint sent it to a one-word search, which found line 88. It took 8 model calls in each of the three runs and got the right answer. A printed table of contents is also a trap, since its page numbers are not line numbers, and the prompt says so at the bottom left.

FAQ

28

The first-rewrite grep agent adds a catalogue, outline, refusals and quote checks. It comes before Trace Fixes. A zero-match result used to look final. Now the tool says zero matches does not show absence and lists the languages in the corpus, and the prompt says to translate terms before searching. Be honest about the 11 calls. The first eight stayed in the wrong French file, on gas prices, and the grep agent only moved to the energy programme on the ninth. It gets there, but it isn't elegant. The answer stays in French because the prompt asks for the document’s own wording, and it still counts as the Netherlands.

FAQ

29

This is the same line of the same contract, line 13 of the NICE agreement, in two real runs. On the left the search matched, because that line does hold the clause, but the tool printed the first 400 characters of the line and stopped. Those characters are about dispute resolution. Nothing tells the model there are 3,800 more. So the model moves on, and the answer leaves out NICE. On the right the tool prints the text around the match, and the clause is there. It also ends with a marker that gives the length of the line, so the model knows it saw only a part. One caution: the two runs differ in more than this. The model wrote a different search each time, and Trace Fixes brought its other changes too, so this slide shows the mechanism and does not measure this fix alone. I did check one thing: the old pattern matches that line only at the clause, so the new tool would have shown the clause to the old search too. Whether the model would then have named NICE, we did not test. The next slide gives the exact rule. In the hosted runs on the 531 pages Grep Token Reduction, which keeps the same excerpt rule, gets this question right.

Sends short lines whole

A line of 400 characters or fewer goes through uncut.

Finds the model’s pattern

FAQ

30

This answers the obvious question: who decides what the model sees? The model does, through the search it writes. These bars are the same line with three searches. A precise phrase sends 411 characters. A rarer word sends two short excerpts. A common word sends most of the line, 3,685 characters, because the windows merge. The rule is plain code with no ranking: short lines go whole, long lines get 200 characters either side of each match, overlaps merge, and it stops at three separate excerpts. Be honest about the rough edge. On the agreement search the last match falls outside the three excerpts, that is the orange tick on bare background, and the marker gives the line length without saying a match was dropped. The model can still read the line, which returns all of it up to 6,000 characters, and a single search result also stops at 6,000 characters. If the pattern finds nothing in the line, the tool sends the first 400 characters.

The hint lives in the tool response

Tool response, role=tool

0 matches for 'ESDS.*technical order|TO.*ESDS' in file TO_00-25-172CL-5.md.

This does not yet show absence. Try one distinctive word, a synonym, or the wording of the document’s language.

No single line holds all of these terms. Lines holding each term alone:

ESDS: 4 matching lines in 1 files.

technical order|TO: 21 matching lines in 1 files.

Search one term at a time, then read the page that holds it.

Pseudocode

system = rules # fixed, sent every turn

result = search(pattern, file)

if result is empty:

    result += HINT

    if pattern joins terms with .*:

        result += count_each_term()

messages.append(role=tool, result)

Next call in this run

search("ESDS")

88 [page 2]: All ESDS parts shall be handled…

Hosted run: Qwen3.5-9B, 4-bit (fp4), Darkbloom through OpenRouter. Validation question 5, third run, Grep Token Reduction. Output shortened.

FAQ

31

People ask where the hint goes, so here is the exact setup. The left is one real tool response from the fuel checklist question, third run. The white line is what any search tool returns. The amber text is what we add, and it goes in the tool message, not the system prompt. The rules that hold for every question stay in the system prompt: search in the document’s language, read around each hit. The hint holds facts about this one search, such as ESDS appearing on 4 lines, which nobody could write in advance. The next call was a search for ESDS, which found line 88. To measure it we removed the hint and the term counts, kept everything else, and ran the test set three times. As a median across those three runs of 20 questions, with the hint off and then on: empty searches 28 to 26, repeated searches 0 to 1, correct answers 9 to 8 of 20. Why it goes here: the hint says what empty means at the moment the model picks its next call. Now the honest part. It barely moves these searches, and it does not raise the score. Treat it as a cheap default worth testing on your own failures, not a proven gain.

FAQ

32

Open this when someone asks what reading a trace looks like. The contents page says the acronym table is on page 140, and the grep agent starts reading near line 140. At its sixth call it had already read the Annex II table that holds the evidence, and it moved on. It then issues nearly the same read seven times until the budget runs out. A bigger model might do better here, but a read tool that reports real page numbers and refuses repeats costs nothing.

Harness refuses a repeated call

Question: which official in the 2019 OCC Annual Report oversees “compliance and community affairs”?

read(lines 225-254)
line 230 names Morris R. Morgan
read(lines 165-194)

read(lines 228-237)
Lines 228-237 are already above. Read other lines, search again, or answer.
read(lines 228-237)

harness, tools removed:

answer: Morris R. Morgan, correct

Skips the tool

The reply says why and what to try instead.

Spares the budget

A refused call uses none of the 20-call budget.

Stops after two turns

After two turns of refused calls, the tools go away and the model must answer.

Hosted run: Qwen3.5-9B, 4-bit (fp4), Darkbloom through OpenRouter. Validation question 13, first run, Trace Fixes. Question and output shortened.

FAQ

33

A refused call is a tool call the harness declines to run, because the model already has the result. There are two kinds: the exact same call again, or a read of lines already on screen. This one is a real trace from the 2019 OCC annual report. The model finds Morris R. Morgan on line 230 and drafts a correct answer. A review turn asks it to check, so it asks for lines 228 to 237, which sit inside what it already read. The harness says so and does not run the call. The model sends the same call again and is told that too. That makes two turns in a row, so the harness takes the tools away and asks for the answer, and the answer is correct. Before this stop, the same habit used all 20 calls and ended in not_found on a question from an earlier set. The refusal finds nothing new; it ends the loop. This is common: as a median across 3 runs, 15 of the 20 Trace Fixes test answers held a refused call, and 14 ended through this stop. Grep Token Reduction later removed the review turn that prompted the repeat here.

FAQ

36

These are the exact names, so you can reproduce it. The vector store does exact search, so nothing here is an approximate-index artefact: a miss is a miss of the embedding, not of the index. We timed Voyager, LanceDB and Chroma on these same vectors. Voyager saves three hundredths of a millisecond and loses three percent of the true top five. LanceDB and Chroma took 2 to 4 milliseconds. A question takes 15 seconds, so the index was never the slow part. The small embedding model runs on the same laptop.
